title: Hawking radiation
part: IV: Orbits, stars, and black holes
one_line_summary: A short, heuristic tour of semiclassical black-hole physics: a vacuum pair split by the horizon explains why black holes glow, an uncertainty-plus-redshift estimate gives an emitted energy of order hbar/M, and the result is promoted to a black-body temperature, evaporation law, surface gravity, Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, the four laws of black-hole mechanics, the generalized second law, the information puzzle and the Unruh effect.
role_in_book: The only quantum-flavoured chapter of Part IV and its second-to-last chapter (Chapter 29 on charged and rotating holes closes the part). Chapters 21-27 built the Schwarzschild geometry, geodesic conserved quantities, Eddington-Finkelstein and Kruskal coordinates and Penrose diagrams as purely classical tools; this chapter cashes them in to show that horizons have thermodynamic properties once quantum fields are allowed. It relies on the Killing-vector energy -p.xi, the swap of timelike and spacelike character across r = 2M, ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates for the surface-gravity calculation, and the Rindler picture from Chapter 26. It sets up Chapter 29 (Omega and Phi in the first law belong to rotating and charged holes) and points ahead to quantum gravity (Chapter 49) as the missing ingredient for the end state of evaporation. It is deliberately qualitative: no quantum field theory in curved spacetime is done, and the rigorous numbers are quoted.

assumed_background.topic: Schwarzschild metric, the horizon at r = 2M and the exchange of roles of t and r inside it
Conserved energy and angular momentum per unit mass (E-tilde, L-tilde) and the radial energy equation with an effective potential
Energy equation for photons with impact parameter b = L/E
Energy measured by an observer as -p.u and the four-momentum mass shell p.p = -m^2
Killing vectors as generators of conserved quantities along geodesics; covariant derivatives and connection coefficients
Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates (V, r, theta, phi)
Rindler coordinates for uniformly accelerated observers and their horizon
Cosmic microwave background and its 2.73 K temperature
Heisenberg energy-time uncertainty, virtual particles, antiparticles and unitary time evolution
Black-body radiation and the Stefan-Boltzmann law (power proportional to area times T^4)
Laws of thermodynamics, entropy as conjugate to temperature, heat capacity
Separable first-order ODEs (solving dM/dt proportional to -1/M^2)
Wick rotation to Euclidean time and periodic imaginary time as temperature (only for Exercise 28.4)

learning_objectives: Reader can describe the pair-creation picture of Hawking radiation: a virtual pair produced just outside the horizon, one member crossing inside, the other escaping as real radiation.

Reader can explain why the conserved Killing energy -p.xi may be negative for a particle inside the horizon without any locally measured negative energy, using the sign change of xi.xi = g_tt at r = 2M.
Reader can show that a photon on a radial plunge with u^t = 0 inside the horizon has positive locally measured energy exactly when p^r < 0.

Reader can reproduce the order-of-magnitude estimate E_infinity ~ hbar/4M from the proper time to fall from 2M + epsilon to the horizon, the uncertainty relation and the redshift factor g^tt, and explain why epsilon cancels.
Reader can quote the Hawking temperature k_B T = hbar/(8 pi M) (and its SI form), evaluate it for a solar-mass hole, and compare it with the CMB temperature.
Reader can derive the scalings L proportional to M^-2 and lifetime proportional to M^3 from Stefan-Boltzmann with horizon area 16 pi M^2, and explain the negative heat capacity.
Reader can define surface gravity through xi^mu xi^nu_{;mu} = kappa xi^nu on a Killing horizon and compute kappa = 1/4M for Schwarzschild in ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates.
Reader can obtain S = k_B A/(4 hbar) by matching dM = T dS with dA = 32 pi M dM, and state the four laws of black-hole mechanics with their thermodynamic counterparts.
Reader can explain why Hawking evaporation violates the classical area theorem and how the generalized second law restores entropy bookkeeping.
Reader can state the black-hole information problem, the candidate end states mentioned (complete evaporation, remnant, final burst), and read the Penrose diagram of an evaporating hole.
Reader can connect Hawking radiation to the Unruh effect via the near-horizon Rindler form of Schwarzschild, and quote T_Unruh = hbar a/(2 pi c k_B).

Reader can carry out the Euclidean near-horizon argument: rewrite the metric as flat polar coordinates after Wick rotation and read off the temperature from the required periodicity of imaginary time.

teaching_approach.summary: An openly heuristic, example-led chapter. Instead of quantum field theory in curved spacetime, the authors run a chain of short classical-GR calculations dressed with one quantum ingredient (the energy-time uncertainty relation) to make Hawking radiation plausible and to get its scale, then quote the exact result and spend the second half on thermodynamic consequences stated as analogies and laws. Heavy lifting is pushed into margin notes (Killing horizons, CMB feeding, thermodynamic dictionary) and exercises (horizon area, heat capacity, surface gravity via Killing's equation, Euclidean temperature). The tone is informal, with jokes about BBC polls, a spoof newspaper and cooking steak by acceleration.
narrative_arc: Motivating claim: black holes are not purely absorbers; they glow like black bodies because the quantum vacuum fluctuates.
Quantum ingredient: virtual pairs are off the mass shell and live for a time set by the uncertainty relation.
Mechanism picture (Fig. 28.1): the horizon can split a pair, freeing both members.
Physical constraint: locally measured energy -p.u must be positive to protect causality.
Check inside the horizon (Example 28.1): a plunging observer finds infalling photons have positive local energy with no constraint on p^t, so the partner is freed.
Energy at infinity: -p.xi can be negative inside because xi turns spacelike, so the infalling member carries negative Killing energy and the escaping one positive.
Estimate (Example 28.2): uncertainty-limited energy near 2M + epsilon redshifted to infinity gives hbar/4M.
Quote the rigorous answer: thermal spectrum with k_B T = hbar/8 pi M.
Consequence (Example 28.3): Stefan-Boltzmann gives dM/dt proportional to -M^-2 and lifetime proportional to M^3; margin note on CMB feeding.
Geometry of temperature: define surface gravity via Killing horizon and compute kappa = 1/4M (Example 28.4), so k_B T = hbar kappa/2 pi.
Entropy from the first law: area plays the role of entropy, S = k_B A/4 hbar.
Generalize: the four laws of black-hole mechanics and a thermodynamic dictionary.
Puzzles: evaporation shrinks area, requiring the generalized second law; information loss threatens unitarity; the end state needs quantum gravity (Example 28.5, Fig. 28.2).
Echo in flat spacetime: near-horizon Rindler form and the Unruh effect (Example 28.6, Fig. 28.3).
Exercises close the loop: horizon area, negative heat capacity, the full surface-gravity computation, and the Euclidean derivation of the exact Hawking temperature.
signature_moves: Replace a quantum field theory calculation by a semiclassical estimate whose free parameter (the distance epsilon above the horizon) cancels, so the answer is forced to scale as hbar/M.
Distinguish the locally measured energy -p.u (always positive) from the Killing energy -p.xi (sign-indefinite inside the horizon) to defuse the negative-energy worry.
Choose the simplest possible interior observer (u^t = 0 radial plunge) so that a single component survives the inner product.
Promote an estimate to a law by quoting the exact result and immediately extracting scaling consequences (T proportional to 1/M, lifetime proportional to M^3).
Build entropy by reading the first law of thermodynamics backwards from dM expressed in terms of dA.
Side-by-side lists: laws of black-hole mechanics in the text, ordinary thermodynamic laws in the margin, then an explicit dictionary.
Use the Rindler wedge to rerun the pair-splitting story in flat spacetime, turning Hawking into Unruh.
Offload the most satisfying rigorous argument (Euclidean periodicity) to a scaffolded exercise.

sections.title: Chapter opening: vacuum fluctuations and virtual pairs
sections.summary: Announces Hawking's 1974 result that black holes emit thermal radiation and names quantum field theory as its proper home. Introduces the quantum vacuum as a ground state that still fluctuates, producing short-lived particle-antiparticle pairs whose borrowed energy and lifetime obey an uncertainty relation, and explains that such virtual particles violate the mass-shell condition p.p = -m^2.
key_moves: Frames Hawking radiation as a quantum effect that classical GR alone cannot produce.
Links the finite pair lifetime to the energy borrowed from the vacuum via Delta E Delta t ~ hbar.
Characterizes virtual particles as off-shell, so their energy is not fixed by the usual dispersion relation.

sections.title: Hawking radiation
sections.summary: Pictures Hawking emission as a vacuum pair born just outside r = 2M in which one member crosses the horizon and the other escapes. Imposes positivity of locally measured energy -p.u, then (Example 28.1) shows that for an observer plunging inside the horizon with u^t = 0 an infalling photon has positive local energy whatever its p^t, so it can propagate freely and release its partner. Next it considers the Killing energy -p.xi measured by an observer at infinity: since xi = e_t becomes spacelike inside the horizon, the infalling member may carry negative Killing energy while the escaping one carries an equal positive amount, conserving energy at infinity. Example 28.2 estimates the escaping energy from the proper time of fall from 2M + epsilon, the uncertainty relation and the static redshift factor, obtaining hbar/4M. The section ends by noting that the rigorous calculation gives a similar answer.
concepts: timelike Killing vector turning spacelike inside the horizon
negative Killing energy inside the horizon
radial plunge with zero Killing energy inside the horizon
key_moves: Require E_obs = -p.u > 0 for any physical propagation, justified by causality.
Inside r < 2M pick u = u^r e_r with u^r = -(2M/r - 1)^{1/2} from u.u = -1 (eqn 28.1).
Evaluate E_obs = -(2M/r - 1)^{-1/2} p^r (eqn 28.2): positive for any infalling photon, with p^t unconstrained, so the uncertainty-imposed lifetime no longer applies.
Note xi.xi = g_tt = -(1 - 2M/r) flips sign at the horizon, so -p.xi can be negative inside without being unphysical.
Energy conservation at infinity then forces the negative-Killing-energy member to fall in and the positive one to escape.
Use a frame momentarily at rest at 2M + epsilon: E-tilde ~ (epsilon/2M)^{1/2} (28.4), proper fall time ~ 2(2M epsilon)^{1/2} (28.5), local energy ~ hbar over that time (28.6).
Relate local and infinity energies through E_obs = -g^{tt} E_inf E-tilde with g^{tt} ~ -2M/epsilon (28.7-28.8); epsilon cancels, leaving E_inf = hbar/4M (28.10).

sections.title: Black-hole thermodynamics
sections.summary: Quotes the exact result that the emitted spectrum is thermal with k_B T = hbar/8 pi M. Example 28.3 uses the black-body law with area 16 pi M^2 to get dM/dt proportional to -1/M^2 and a lifetime scaling as M^3; a long margin note explains that the CMB keeps feeding real holes, so only holes below about 2.3 x 10^-8 solar masses (roughly 4.5 x 10^22 kg; the book's kg figure is misprinted as 10^23) could currently shrink. Surface gravity is defined geometrically on a Killing horizon (eqn 28.13) and computed in ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates as kappa = 1/4M (Example 28.4), giving k_B T = hbar kappa/2 pi. Matching dM written in terms of dA against dU = T dS identifies entropy S = k_B A/4 hbar.
concepts: negative heat capacity of black holes
black holes in the cosmic microwave background
key_moves: Replace the estimate hbar/4M by the exact thermal result k_B T = hbar/8 pi M.
Luminosity proportional to A T^4 with A = 16 pi M^2 and T proportional to 1/M gives L proportional to M^-2; integrating dM/dt gives lifetime proportional to M^3.
Compare T for one solar mass (62 nK) with T_CMB = 2.73 K to show astrophysical holes grow.
Define kappa by xi^mu xi^nu_{;mu} = kappa xi^nu on the horizon, lower the index of xi = partial_V to get xi_nu = (-1 + 2M/r, 1, 0, 0), and evaluate to kappa = 1/4M.
Conclude k_B T = hbar kappa/2 pi.
Write dM = dA/(32 pi M) = [hbar/(8 pi k_B M)] d(k_B A/4 hbar) and read off S.

sections.title: Within 28.2: laws of black-hole mechanics, generalized second law and information
sections.summary: States four laws for a hole with mass M, angular momentum L, charge q, area A and surface gravity kappa (kappa uniform on the horizon; dM = kappa dA/8 pi + Omega dL + Phi dq; area never decreases; kappa cannot be driven to zero in finitely many steps), with the ordinary laws of thermodynamics and a variable dictionary in the margin. Notes that merging holes cannot lose total area and that swallowing matter increases the hole's entropy. Because evaporation shrinks the area, it introduces the generalized second law for hole plus environment. It then raises the information problem (apparent loss of unitarity), mentions remnant and explosion proposals and Hawking's view that information is lost, and (Example 28.5) shows the Penrose diagram of a completely evaporating hole while stressing that the final stage needs quantum gravity.
concepts: Penrose diagram of an evaporating black hole
quantum gravity at the end of evaporation
key_moves: Pair each black-hole law with its thermodynamic twin (margin notes 16-17).
Apply the area law to black-hole mergers: final area at least the sum of initial areas.
Recognize that Hawking emission violates dA >= 0 and repair the second law by counting radiation entropy.
Frame information loss as a clash with unitary evolution and list proposed escapes.
Accept complete evaporation provisionally to draw the corresponding Penrose diagram.

sections.title: Within 28.2: Unruh effect and chapter summary
sections.summary: Recalls that near the horizon Schwarzschild coordinates behave like accelerated coordinates in Minkowski space, and introduces the Unruh effect: a uniformly accelerated observer in vacuum detects thermal radiation at k_B T = hbar a/(2 pi c) while an inertial observer detects none. Example 28.6 writes the near-horizon metric in Rindler form, identifies T = +-X as the accelerated observer's horizon (Fig. 28.3), reruns the pair-splitting story across that horizon, and estimates the temperature by dimensional analysis. The chapter summary recaps emission, T proportional to 1/M and the thermodynamic analogy.
key_moves: Map near-horizon Schwarzschild to the Rindler line element ds^2 = -x^2 dt^2 + dx^2.
Observers at fixed Rindler x are hyperbolae in the wedge X > |T|; nothing from X < |T| reaches them, so T = +-X acts as a horizon.
Split a vacuum pair across T = X: the partner left in X > |T| is Unruh radiation.
Dimensional analysis gives k_B T ~ hbar a/c, consistent with the exact hbar a/(2 pi c).

sections.title: Exercises: area, heat capacity, surface gravity and the Euclidean temperature
sections.summary: Four exercises finish the chapter's sketches: integrate the horizon area, find the (negative) heat capacity, complete the Eddington-Finkelstein surface-gravity computation using Killing's equation and a covariant-derivative rule, and derive the exact Hawking temperature by expanding Schwarzschild near r = 2M, Wick-rotating, and demanding that the resulting flat polar geometry be free of a conical defect.
concepts: negative heat capacity of black holes
key_moves: Use Killing's equation to rewrite the surface-gravity definition as -xi^mu xi_mu^{;sigma} = kappa xi^sigma and reduce it to xi_{V;r} = -kappa.
Use Gamma^V_{rV} = 0 and Gamma^r_{rV} = -M/r^2 to recover eqn 28.15.
Substitute rho^2 = 8M(r - 2M) to obtain Rindler-like form, set t = -i t_E and t_E = 4M psi to get d rho^2 + rho^2 d psi^2.
Require psi to have period 2 pi so that t_E has period 8 pi M, identifying hbar/k_B T = 8 pi M.

concepts.name: vacuum fluctuations
concepts.definition: In quantum field theory the lowest-energy state of a field (the vacuum, containing no real particles) is not static: it continually and briefly produces particle-antiparticle pairs that recombine.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening paragraph, as the physical source of Hawking radiation, described in words with no field theory formalism.

concepts.name: virtual particles
concepts.definition: Transient particles in intermediate states whose four-momentum does not satisfy p.p = -m^2; the energy excess they borrow limits their lifetime to roughly hbar divided by that energy.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced right after vacuum fluctuations to explain why pairs must annihilate quickly; the off-shell property explains why their energy is not fixed by the dispersion relation.
concepts.notes: The printed opening writes the lifetime as Delta E/hbar; it should be hbar/Delta E (correctly given later on the same page).

concepts.name: mass shell
concepts.definition: A free particle of rest mass m has four-momentum obeying p.p = -m^2 (signature -+++), i.e. E^2 = |p|^2 + m^2 in an inertial frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled to define what it means for virtual particles to be off shell; margin note 2 uses the two roots E = +-(p^2 + m^2)^{1/2} to discuss antiparticles.

concepts.name: energy-time uncertainty relation
concepts.definition: Heuristic quantum relation Delta E Delta t ~ hbar linking the energy uncertainty of a transient state to its duration; used to bound how long a vacuum pair can exist.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked in the opening and again in Example 28.2 to assign an energy hbar/Delta tau to a photon that exists for the proper time a frame takes to fall to the horizon.
concepts.notes: Time is not an operator, so this is an order-of-magnitude statement rather than a strict inequality.

concepts.name: antiparticle positive energy
concepts.definition: Every observed particle and antiparticle has positive energy; the negative root of the dispersion relation is reinterpreted as a positive-energy antiparticle with reversed three-momentum, equivalently a negative-energy state running backward in time.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin notes 2 and 3 correct the common claim that antiparticles carry negative energy, using the four-momentum flip (-E, p) to (E, -p) and the wavefunction phase exp(-iEt/hbar).

concepts.name: positivity of locally measured energy
concepts.definition: Any real particle or photon must have positive energy E_obs = -p.u as measured by a local observer with four-velocity u; otherwise it would effectively travel backward in time and threaten causality.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the key physical requirement in section 28.1 and used as the test for whether a photon can propagate inside the horizon (Example 28.1).

concepts.name: observer-measured energy
concepts.definition: The energy of a particle with four-momentum p as measured by an observer with four-velocity u is E_obs = -p.u, the time component of p in that observer's local inertial frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from earlier chapters and used twice: for the plunging interior observer (Example 28.1) and for a frame momentarily at rest just outside the horizon (Example 28.2).

concepts.name: Killing energy
concepts.definition: For a stationary spacetime with timelike Killing vector xi = partial_t, the quantity -p.xi = -p_t is conserved along a geodesic and equals the energy that a static observer at infinity (whose four-velocity is xi there) would measure.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note 6 identifies the static observer at infinity with xi^mu = (1,0,0,0) and relates E-tilde = -xi.u to E = -xi.p; the text then argues about its sign across the horizon.

concepts.name: timelike Killing vector turning spacelike inside the horizon
aliases: sign flip of g_tt at r = 2M
concepts.definition: The Schwarzschild Killing vector xi = e_t has norm xi.xi = g_tt = -(1 - 2M/r), negative (timelike) for r > 2M, null at r = 2M and positive (spacelike) for r < 2M.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note 7, used to explain why a negative value of -p.xi is not forbidden inside the horizon: there, -p.xi is a momentum-like component rather than an energy anyone measures.

concepts.name: negative Killing energy inside the horizon
aliases: negative energy at infinity for infalling partner
concepts.definition: Inside a black hole a particle can have -p.xi < 0 while every local observer still measures positive energy; the infalling member of a Hawking pair carries such negative Killing energy, so the hole's mass decreases by the energy the escaping partner takes to infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Argued in section 28.1 from the norm flip of xi and energy conservation for the observer at infinity, then reused in 28.2 to explain the loss of mass.
prerequisites: timelike Killing vector turning spacelike inside the horizon
concepts.notes: Same geometric mechanism as the Penrose process in the ergoregion of a Kerr hole (not mentioned in this chapter).

concepts.name: radial plunge with zero Killing energy inside the horizon
concepts.definition: Inside r < 2M, r is a time coordinate, so an observer can move with only u^r non-zero; normalization u.u = -1 then gives u^r = -(2M/r - 1)^{1/2}, a timelike path with E-tilde = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Chosen in Example 28.1 as the simplest interior observer so that the inner product p.u reduces to a single g_rr p^r u^r term.

concepts.name: Hawking radiation
concepts.definition: Quantum emission of particles by a black-hole horizon with a thermal (black-body) spectrum at temperature k_B T = hbar c^3/(8 pi G M); the energy carried off reduces the hole's mass.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as a surprising 1974 result, made plausible by the pair-splitting picture and a redshift estimate, then quoted exactly at the start of section 28.2.
prerequisites: negative Killing energy inside the horizon
concepts.notes: Not yet observed, as the book notes. The heuristic picture gets the scale but not the spectrum or the 2 pi.

concepts.name: horizon pair-splitting picture
concepts.definition: Cartoon model in which a vacuum pair forms just outside the horizon; one member crosses r = 2M and is no longer forced to recombine, so the other escapes as real radiation.
concepts.how_introduced: Fig. 28.1 and the opening of 28.1, justified by Examples 28.1-28.2 and later rerun across the Rindler horizon for the Unruh effect.
concepts.notes: A heuristic: the actual derivation compares vacuum states at past and future infinity (Bogoliubov coefficients) and the emission is not localized at the horizon.

concepts.name: gravitational redshift near the horizon
concepts.definition: A quantum of energy E_inf at infinity is measured by a static observer at radius r to have energy E_inf (1 - 2M/r)^{-1/2}; near r = 2M + epsilon this factor is about (2M/epsilon)^{1/2}.
concepts.how_introduced: Implicit in Example 28.2: the combination -g^{tt} E-tilde with g^{tt} ~ -2M/epsilon and E-tilde ~ (epsilon/2M)^{1/2} is exactly this factor, which lets the near-horizon energy be carried to infinity.
concepts.notes: The book does not use the word redshift here; naming it helps learners connect to earlier chapters.

concepts.name: radial energy equation for geodesics
concepts.definition: For radial Schwarzschild motion, (dr/dtau)^2 = E-tilde^2 - 1 + 2M/r for massive particles, and for photons 1/b^2 = (1/L^2)(dr/dlambda)^2 + (1/r^2)(1 - 2M/r), which for zero angular momentum gives E-tilde = +-dr/dlambda.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in margin notes 5 and 9 to fix E-tilde for a frame at rest at 2M + epsilon and to compute the proper time to fall to the horizon.

concepts.name: Hawking temperature
concepts.definition: Temperature of the thermal spectrum emitted by a Schwarzschild hole, k_B T = hbar/(8 pi M) in G = c = 1 units, i.e. T = hbar c^3/(8 pi G M k_B), about 62 nK for one solar mass; it rises as the mass falls.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted as the rigorous result after the hbar/4M estimate, then re-expressed through surface gravity (k_B T = hbar kappa/2 pi) and derived in Exercise 28.4 from Euclidean periodicity.
concepts.notes: The book writes approximately equal in eqn 28.11, but for Schwarzschild the relation is exact.

concepts.name: Stefan-Boltzmann law
concepts.definition: A black body of area A at temperature T radiates power proportional to A T^4.
concepts.how_introduced: Used in Example 28.3 with A = 16 pi M^2 to find how quickly a hole loses mass.
concepts.notes: Real Hawking emission is modified by greybody factors and the number of particle species; the book ignores both.

concepts.name: black-hole evaporation
concepts.definition: An isolated black hole loses mass through Hawking emission at a rate proportional to 1/M^2, growing hotter as it shrinks, so its total lifetime scales as M^3.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 28.3 combines T proportional to 1/M with the Stefan-Boltzmann law; the end state is discussed with Fig. 28.2 and Example 28.5.

concepts.name: negative heat capacity of black holes
concepts.definition: Because T is proportional to 1/M, adding energy cools a Schwarzschild hole and removing energy heats it, so C = dM/dT = -hbar/(8 pi k_B T^2) (G = c = 1) is negative, which makes evaporation a runaway and prevents stable equilibrium with an infinite bath.
concepts.how_introduced: Only in Exercise 28.2, where the reader must find C and explain the minus sign.
concepts.notes: Printed eqn 28.23 gives -hbar^2/(16 pi k_B T^2); direct differentiation gives -hbar/(8 pi k_B T^2) = -2S (see gaps).

concepts.name: black holes in the cosmic microwave background
concepts.definition: A black hole colder than the 2.73 K CMB absorbs more radiation than it emits and so grows; only holes lighter than about 4.5 x 10^22 kg are currently hotter than the CMB.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note 12 attached to the evaporation estimate, using the solar-mass temperature and the mass at which T equals T_CMB.
concepts.notes: Book prints M_CMB = 4.5 x 10^23 kg; the correct conversion of 2.3 x 10^-8 solar masses is 4.5 x 10^22 kg.

concepts.name: surface gravity
concepts.definition: For a Killing horizon generated by a Killing vector xi normalized at infinity, kappa is defined by xi^mu nabla_mu xi^nu = kappa xi^nu on the horizon; physically it is the force per unit mass that must be applied from infinity to hold a test body at the horizon (the redshifted acceleration). For Schwarzschild kappa = 1/4M.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the geometric counterpart of temperature, defined by eqn 28.13, explained in margin note 13 and computed in Example 28.4 and Exercise 28.3.
concepts.notes: kappa depends on the normalization of xi, which is why the Killing vector is fixed to have unit norm at infinity; the local proper acceleration of a hovering observer diverges at the horizon.

concepts.name: Killing horizon
concepts.definition: A null hypersurface on which some Killing vector field is null and normal to the surface; for static black holes it coincides with the event horizon.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin notes 13-14: described as a geometric upgrade of the event horizon; the Schwarzschild field xi_nu = (-1 + 2M/r, 1, 0, 0) is null at r = 2M.

concepts.name: Killing's equation
concepts.definition: A vector field xi is a Killing vector (generates an isometry) if and only if xi_{mu;nu} + xi_{nu;mu} = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Used only in Exercise 28.3 to move the derivative index and obtain an alternative form of the surface-gravity condition.

concepts.name: ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates built from the advanced null time V so that the Schwarzschild metric ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/r) dV^2 + 2 dV dr + r^2 dOmega^2 is regular at r = 2M.
concepts.how_introduced: Reused from Chapter 26 because surface gravity must be evaluated on the horizon, where Schwarzschild coordinates fail; partial_V keeps components (1,0,0,0).

concepts.name: Bekenstein-Hawking entropy
concepts.definition: Entropy of a black hole proportional to its horizon area, S = k_B A/(4 hbar) in G = c = 1 units, i.e. S = k_B c^3 A/(4 G hbar) = k_B A/(4 l_P^2).
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by rewriting dM for a Schwarzschild hole in terms of dA and matching to dU = T dS with T the Hawking temperature.
prerequisites: horizon area of Schwarzschild black hole
concepts.notes: The book does not name Bekenstein, whose 1973 area-entropy proposal preceded Hawking's temperature.

concepts.name: horizon area of Schwarzschild black hole
concepts.definition: The proper area of the r = 2M sphere, A = 4 pi (2M)^2 = 16 pi M^2, obtained by integrating r^2 sin theta dtheta dphi from the metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in Example 28.3 and set as Exercise 28.1.

concepts.name: first law of thermodynamics
concepts.definition: Change in internal energy equals heat absorbed T dS plus work done on the system (dU = T dS - p dV).
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the template for identifying black-hole entropy and listed in margin note 16 with the other thermodynamic laws.

concepts.name: laws of black-hole mechanics
concepts.definition: Four statements for stationary black holes that mirror thermodynamics: kappa is uniform on the horizon (zeroth), dM = kappa dA/8 pi + Omega dL + Phi dq (first), horizon area does not decrease classically (second), and kappa cannot be reduced to zero in finitely many steps (third).
concepts.how_introduced: Listed after the entropy identification, with the ordinary thermodynamic laws in margin note 16 and a dictionary (M-U, kappa-T, A-S, work terms) in margin note 17.

concepts.name: zeroth law of black-hole mechanics
concepts.definition: The surface gravity of a stationary black hole takes the same value everywhere on its horizon, analogous to uniform temperature in equilibrium.
concepts.how_introduced: First entry in the list of four laws.

concepts.name: first law of black-hole mechanics
concepts.definition: Neighbouring stationary black holes differing by dM, dL, dq satisfy dM = (kappa/8 pi) dA + Omega dL + Phi dq, where Omega is the horizon angular velocity and Phi the horizon electric potential.
concepts.how_introduced: Second entry in the list; generalizes the Schwarzschild entropy calculation to rotating and charged holes (developed in Chapter 29).
prerequisites: horizon area of Schwarzschild black hole

concepts.name: Hawking area theorem
concepts.definition: Classically (with matter obeying the null energy condition) the total area of black-hole horizons never decreases, so merging holes produce a final area at least equal to the sum of the initial areas.
concepts.how_introduced: Third entry in the list, applied to colliding holes and to matter falling in; then shown to fail for evaporation.
prerequisites: horizon area of Schwarzschild black hole
concepts.notes: The book does not state the energy-condition hypothesis, which is exactly what Hawking radiation violates.

concepts.name: third law of black-hole mechanics
concepts.definition: No finite sequence of operations can reduce a black hole's surface gravity to zero (reach an extremal hole), analogous to the unattainability of absolute zero.
concepts.how_introduced: Fourth entry in the list.

concepts.name: generalized second law
concepts.definition: The sum of black-hole entropy (k_B A/4 hbar) and the ordinary entropy outside the hole never decreases.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced because Hawking evaporation shrinks the horizon area, violating dA >= 0; the radiation's entropy is argued to compensate once thermalized with the environment.

concepts.name: black-hole information problem
concepts.definition: If a black hole evaporates completely, the quantum information carried by what fell in appears to be destroyed, which would break the unitary (reversible) evolution of quantum mechanics.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised after the GSL as an open worry; the book lists remnants and a final explosion as proposed escapes and records Hawking's view that information is lost.
concepts.notes: Treatment is brief and pre-dates later developments (complementarity, firewalls, Page curve and island calculations).

concepts.name: unitarity of quantum evolution
concepts.definition: Quantum states evolve by unitary operators, so a later state determines the earlier one and vice versa; information is never destroyed.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked to explain why information loss would be troubling.

concepts.name: Penrose diagram of an evaporating black hole
concepts.definition: Conformal diagram of a star collapsing to a hole that later evaporates completely: an event horizon and a spacelike singularity exist only for a finite stretch, after which the regular centre r = 0 continues up to future timelike infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 28.5, with Fig. 28.2, drawn on the provisional assumption that the hole disappears.

concepts.name: quantum gravity at the end of evaporation
concepts.definition: When a hole shrinks toward the Planck scale, classical GR (with quantum fields on a fixed background) should break down, so the final stage of evaporation requires an as-yet incomplete theory of quantum gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 28.5, pointing ahead to Chapter 49.

concepts.name: Unruh effect
concepts.definition: A uniformly accelerated observer in the Minkowski vacuum detects a thermal bath at temperature hbar a/(2 pi c k_B), while an inertial observer detects none; particle content is observer-dependent.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the resemblance between near-horizon Schwarzschild and accelerated coordinates; Example 28.6 reruns the pair-splitting story across the Rindler horizon.

concepts.name: Unruh temperature
concepts.definition: Temperature k_B T = hbar a/(2 pi c) perceived by an observer with proper acceleration a; for a = g it is about 4 x 10^-20 K.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted in the text, estimated as hbar a/c by dimensional analysis in Example 28.6, and joked about in margin note 20.
concepts.notes: Setting a = kappa reproduces the Hawking temperature, which is the point of the analogy.

concepts.name: Rindler coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates adapted to uniformly accelerated observers covering the wedge X > |T| of Minkowski space, with line element ds^2 = -x^2 dt^2 + dx^2; each fixed x is a hyperbola with proper acceleration 1/x.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 26 in Example 28.6 as the near-horizon form of Schwarzschild.

concepts.name: Rindler horizon
concepts.definition: The null lines T = +-X bounding the Rindler wedge: events beyond them can never send signals to (or receive them from) the uniformly accelerated observer, so they act as an event horizon.
concepts.how_introduced: Fig. 28.3 and Example 28.6, where a pair is split across T = X.

concepts.name: near-horizon Rindler approximation
concepts.definition: Close to r = 2M, with proper distance rho = [8M(r - 2M)]^{1/2}, the t-r part of Schwarzschild becomes -(rho/4M)^2 dt^2 + d rho^2, i.e. Rindler space with acceleration parameter kappa = 1/4M times a 2-sphere of radius 2M.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in Example 28.6 and derived step by step in Exercise 28.4(a)-(b).

concepts.name: Wick rotation and Euclidean periodicity
concepts.definition: Continuing t = -i t_E turns the near-horizon metric into flat 2D polar form d rho^2 + rho^2 d psi^2 with psi = t_E/4M; smoothness at rho = 0 requires psi to have period 2 pi, so t_E has period 8 pi M, and in thermal field theory an imaginary-time period hbar/k_B T means k_B T = hbar/8 pi M.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 28.4 with a short italic explanation and a pointer to Zee.
concepts.notes: The book never names the conical-defect argument; it just asks the reader to interpret psi as an angle.

concepts.name: geometric units with hbar and k_B retained
concepts.definition: G = c = 1 throughout, but hbar and k_B are kept explicitly so that quantum and thermal factors remain visible; c reappears in the quoted Unruh temperature.
concepts.how_introduced: Implicit in all formulas, e.g. E = hbar/4M, k_B T = hbar/8 pi M, S = A k_B/4 hbar.

key_equations.name: Energy-time uncertainty for virtual pairs
key_equations.meaning: The energy borrowed from the vacuum and the pair's lifetime are inversely related.
key_equations.symbols: Delta E borrowed energy; Delta t pair lifetime

key_equations.name: Mass shell
key_equations.meaning: Real particles satisfy this; virtual particles do not.

key_equations.name: Pair lifetime (corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Maximum lifetime of a virtual pair. The printed opening has Delta E/hbar, a slip; the correct form appears in 28.1.

key_equations.name: Locally measured energy
key_equations.meaning: Energy of a particle in the rest frame of an observer with four-velocity u; must be positive.

key_equations.name: Dispersion relation roots
key_equations.meaning: Two roots whose negative branch is reinterpreted as a positive-energy antiparticle with reversed momentum (margin note 2).

key_equations.name: Photon energy equation
key_equations.meaning: Recalled radial photon equation; for a radial photon the conserved energy equals plus or minus p^r.
key_equations.symbols: b = L/E impact parameter; lambda affine parameter

key_equations.name: Killing energies
key_equations.meaning: Energy per unit mass and total energy conserved along geodesics; equals the energy measured by a static observer at infinity.
key_equations.symbols: xi = e_t Killing vector; u four-velocity; p = m u

key_equations.name: Norm of the time Killing vector
key_equations.meaning: xi is timelike outside, null on, and spacelike inside the horizon, so -p.xi need not be positive inside.

key_equations.name: Interior plunge velocity
key_equations.meaning: Radial velocity of an interior observer with u^t = 0, from u.u = -1 with g_rr = (1 - 2M/r)^{-1}.

key_equations.name: Local photon energy inside the horizon
key_equations.meaning: Positive whenever p^r < 0 (any infalling photon), with no restriction on p^t, so the photon propagates freely.

key_equations.name: Energy at infinity
key_equations.meaning: Conserved along the geodesic; for the escaping member it is what the distant observer measures.

key_equations.name: Radial energy equation
key_equations.meaning: Radial free fall with zero angular momentum (from margin note 9); used to fix E-tilde and the fall time.

key_equations.name: Energy of frame at rest at 2M + epsilon
key_equations.meaning: A frame momentarily at rest just above the horizon has tiny Killing energy per unit mass.
key_equations.symbols: epsilon small height above 2M in r

key_equations.name: Proper time to fall to the horizon
key_equations.meaning: Lifetime available to the virtual pair before the infalling member crosses r = 2M.

key_equations.name: Uncertainty-limited local energy
key_equations.meaning: Energy of the virtual photon in the local frame, set by the fall time.

key_equations.name: Unit-mass energy from lowered velocity
key_equations.meaning: Margin note 10: the only non-zero lowered component of the momentarily static frame's velocity.

key_equations.name: Local versus infinity energy
key_equations.meaning: Connects the energy measured near the horizon to the conserved energy at infinity; equivalent to the static redshift factor.

key_equations.name: Inverse metric near the horizon
key_equations.meaning: Large redshift factor just above r = 2M.

key_equations.name: Matching condition
key_equations.meaning: Both sides scale as epsilon^{-1/2}, so the arbitrary height cancels.

key_equations.name: Hawking energy estimate
key_equations.meaning: Heuristic energy carried to infinity per quantum; inversely proportional to the hole's mass (restoring constants: hbar c^3/4GM). Exceeds the exact k_B T by a factor 2 pi.

key_equations.name: Hawking temperature
key_equations.meaning: Exact temperature of the thermal spectrum emitted by a Schwarzschild hole (the approximate sign is unnecessary).
key_equations.symbols: k_B Boltzmann constant; M mass (G = c = 1)

key_equations.name: Hawking temperature in SI units
key_equations.meaning: Restored-units version (our addition) matching the 62 nK quoted in margin note 12.

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild horizon area
key_equations.meaning: Proper area of the r = 2M sphere (Exercise 28.1).

key_equations.name: Evaporation rate
key_equations.meaning: Luminosity A T^4 with A proportional to M^2 and T to 1/M; integrating gives a lifetime scaling as the cube of the mass.

key_equations.name: Definition of surface gravity
key_equations.meaning: Along the horizon generator, xi is transported into a multiple of itself; the proportionality factor is the surface gravity.
key_equations.symbols: xi Killing vector null on the horizon; semicolon covariant derivative

key_equations.name: Killing 1-form in ingoing EF coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Lowered components of partial_V; null on r = 2M (margin note 14, Exercise 28.3a).

key_equations.name: Surface gravity equation evaluated
key_equations.meaning: Partial derivative plus connection term; gives M/r^2 which on the horizon equals kappa.

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild surface gravity
key_equations.meaning: Value at r = 2M; restoring units kappa = c^4/4GM.

key_equations.name: Temperature from surface gravity
key_equations.meaning: Temperature is surface gravity times hbar/2 pi; holds for all Killing horizons including Rindler (Unruh).

key_equations.name: Mass change in terms of area
key_equations.meaning: Rewriting dM so that the Hawking temperature multiplies a differential, as in dU = T dS.

key_equations.name: Bekenstein-Hawking entropy
key_equations.meaning: Black-hole entropy is a quarter of horizon area in Planck units.

key_equations.name: First law of black-hole mechanics
key_equations.meaning: Energy change of a stationary hole splits into heat-like area term plus rotational and electrical work terms.
key_equations.symbols: Omega horizon angular velocity; L angular momentum; Phi horizon electric potential; q charge

key_equations.name: Second law of black-hole mechanics
key_equations.meaning: Classical area theorem.

key_equations.name: First law of thermodynamics
key_equations.meaning: Template used in margin note 16.

key_equations.name: Thermodynamic dictionary
key_equations.meaning: Correspondences between black-hole and thermodynamic variables (margin note 17). With the stated convention dW = -p dV the work terms should match +dW, so the printed sign is inconsistent; kappa and A match T and S only up to the factors hbar/2 pi k_B and k_B/4 hbar.

key_equations.name: Unruh temperature
key_equations.meaning: Temperature seen by an observer with proper acceleration a in vacuum.

key_equations.name: Rindler line element
key_equations.meaning: Near-horizon (t, r) geometry and the metric of accelerated observers in Minkowski space.
key_equations.symbols: (t, x) Rindler coordinates; Minkowski (T, X) with ds^2 = -dT^2 + dX^2

key_equations.name: Unruh temperature by dimensional analysis
key_equations.meaning: Only combination of hbar, a and c with dimensions of energy; misses the 2 pi.

key_equations.name: Heat capacity of a Schwarzschild hole (as printed)
key_equations.meaning: Negative heat capacity. Printed right-hand side appears wrong: from S = hbar/(16 pi k_B T^2) one gets C = -2S = -hbar/(8 pi k_B T^2) in G = c = 1 units.

key_equations.name: Heat capacity (corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Our correction of eqn 28.23; SI form -hbar c^5/(8 pi G k_B T^2).

key_equations.name: Killing 1-form (exercise)
key_equations.meaning: Same as 28.14, to be derived by lowering with the ingoing EF metric.

key_equations.name: Killing's equation
key_equations.meaning: Defining property of Killing vectors.

key_equations.name: Alternative surface-gravity condition
key_equations.meaning: Follows from 28.13 by Killing's equation.

key_equations.name: Reduced surface-gravity equation
key_equations.meaning: Component to compute in ingoing EF coordinates.

key_equations.name: Covariant derivative of a 1-form
key_equations.meaning: Rule used with Gamma^V_{rV} = 0 and Gamma^r_{rV} = -M/r^2.

key_equations.name: Near-horizon Schwarzschild metric
key_equations.meaning: Leading behaviour close to r = 2M. Printed d Omega^2 lacks the square on d theta.

key_equations.name: Proper-distance form
key_equations.meaning: Rindler form with acceleration parameter 1/4M.
key_equations.symbols: rho proper radial distance from horizon

key_equations.name: Euclidean near-horizon metric
key_equations.meaning: After Wick rotation the (t_E, rho) plane is flat space in polar coordinates.

key_equations.name: Euclidean periodicity gives Hawking temperature
key_equations.meaning: Answer to Exercise 28.4(d) (our statement): no conical singularity at rho = 0 fixes the temperature exactly.

figures.label: Fig. 28.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Virtual particle-antiparticle pairs appearing and vanishing near a black hole's event horizon.
figures.visual_description: Schematic spacetime sketch with time t up and x to the right (axes at lower left). Two parallel vertical solid lines, each labelled horizon, bound a stippled grey strip; a vertical wavy line labelled singularity runs down its middle. Outside the strip, on each side, sit two small closed lens-shaped loops with arrowheads (a pair created and re-annihilated). Beside each horizon there is also one open pair drawn as a bent line with its kink just outside the horizon. On the left, one arm runs to the horizon while the other rises away from the hole and trails off as dots near the top. On the right, one arm with an arrowhead heads up and outward, while the other continues as a dotted line into the stippled interior. The two sides are similar but not exact mirror images.
figures.what_it_teaches: Most vacuum pairs close up and leave no trace; only pairs straddling the horizon are torn apart, and their outside members make up Hawking radiation.

redesign.idea: Animated field of vacuum loops on an Eddington-Finkelstein style spacetime diagram with tilted light cones: loops far from the horizon close, loops near it are stretched and split, and escaping partners stream to a counter at infinity.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags a probe loop toward the horizon and varies its size (lifetime); a readout shows the proper time to reach the horizon versus the loop lifetime, flags when the pair splits, and shows the Killing energy sign of each member (positive outside, negative for the infalling one).

figures.label: Fig. 28.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Conformal diagram for a spacetime in which a black hole forms by collapse and then evaporates completely.
figures.visual_description: Penrose diagram. The left boundary is a vertical line labelled r = 0 rising from the bottom vertex. A hatched region, bounded by this line and a curve bending up and to the right, is the collapsing star. At the top of the hatched region a short horizontal wavy line marks the singularity. A straight 45-degree line runs from a point on the lower-left r = 0 axis up to the right-hand end of the wavy line: this is the event horizon, and it crosses the star's surface. From the end of the singularity a second vertical line, also labelled r = 0, rises to the top vertex. From the top vertex a line labelled script-I-plus slopes down to the right-hand corner, and from that corner a line labelled script-I-minus slopes back down to the bottom vertex.
figures.what_it_teaches: An evaporating hole has a horizon and singularity of finite extent; after evaporation, space has an ordinary centre again, and the diagram frames the question of where infallen information ends up.
concepts: Penrose diagram of an evaporating black hole
quantum gravity at the end of evaporation

redesign.idea: Morphing Penrose diagram that interpolates between the eternal collapse diagram (Chapter 25/27) and the evaporating one as the evaporation time is dialled from infinite to finite, with light rays that the learner can launch.
redesign.interaction: Learner sets the hole's initial mass (hence lifetime) and clicks events to emit future light cones; rays show which events can reach script-I-plus, the horizon shrinks back as evaporation time decreases, and a toggle overlays a highlighted Cauchy-surface slice before and after evaporation to illustrate the information puzzle.

figures.label: Fig. 28.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: A uniformly accelerated observer traces a hyperbola in Minkowski spacetime; Rindler coordinates cover only a wedge, whose edges form a horizon that the observer hugs more closely at high acceleration.
figures.visual_description: Minkowski diagram with vertical T axis and horizontal X axis crossing at the origin. From the origin two thick straight lines at 45 degrees run up-right and down-right (T = X and T = -X), enclosing a grey shaded wedge X > |T| that opens to the right. Inside the wedge a single thin hyperbola opens to the right: its vertex sits on the X axis a little to the right of the origin and its arms approach the two 45-degree boundary lines asymptotically.
figures.what_it_teaches: The accelerated observer's world line never crosses the null lines T = +-X, so everything beyond them is hidden; this acceleration horizon plays the role of the black-hole horizon in the Unruh effect.

redesign.idea: Rindler wedge explorer linking acceleration, horizon distance and Unruh temperature, with an optional side panel showing the same curves as static observers above a Schwarzschild horizon.
redesign.interaction: Learner slides proper acceleration a: the hyperbola X^2 - T^2 = (c^2/a)^2 moves toward the corner, a light signal launched from beyond T = X never reaches it, and a thermometer shows T_U = hbar a/(2 pi c k_B) on a log scale with markers for a = g and for kappa of solar-mass and asteroid-mass holes; pair loops straddling T = X split in animation.

worked_examples.label: Example 28.1
worked_examples.problem: Show that one member of a virtual photon pair created just outside r = 2M can propagate freely once it is inside the horizon.
worked_examples.method: Adopt an interior observer on a radial plunge with u^t = 0, normalize to get u^r, take a radially infalling photon with E-tilde = +-p^r, and compute E_obs = -g_rr p^r u^r.
worked_examples.key_insight: Inside the horizon the positivity condition constrains only p^r, never p^t, so the uncertainty-imposed lifetime is lifted and the outside partner is released.
concepts: radial plunge with zero Killing energy inside the horizon

worked_examples.label: Example 28.2
worked_examples.problem: Estimate the energy delivered to infinity by the escaping photon of a pair created near the horizon.
worked_examples.method: Use a freely falling frame momentarily at rest at 2M + epsilon; find E-tilde from the radial energy equation, the proper time to fall to r = 2M, and the uncertainty-limited energy; connect to the conserved p_t via E_obs = -g^{tt} E_inf E-tilde with g^{tt} ~ -2M/epsilon.
worked_examples.key_insight: The near-horizon blueshift (2M/epsilon)^{1/2} exactly compensates the epsilon dependence of the lifetime, so the result depends only on M.
worked_examples.result: E_inf = hbar/4M (about 2 pi times the exact k_B T).

worked_examples.label: Example 28.3
worked_examples.problem: Find how the mass and lifetime of an isolated hole scale when it radiates as a black body.
worked_examples.method: Combine power proportional to A T^4, horizon area 16 pi M^2 and T proportional to 1/M; equate power to -dM/dt and integrate.
worked_examples.key_insight: Smaller holes are hotter and radiate faster, so evaporation accelerates; lifetime grows as the cube of the initial mass.

worked_examples.label: Example 28.4
worked_examples.problem: Compute the surface gravity of a Schwarzschild black hole and relate it to its temperature.
worked_examples.method: Work in ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates where xi = partial_V is regular at r = 2M, lower its index to get xi_nu = (-1 + 2M/r, 1, 0, 0), evaluate the definition xi^mu xi^nu_{;mu} = kappa xi^nu including the connection term, and set r = 2M; details in Exercise 28.3.
worked_examples.key_insight: Temperature is geometric: k_B T is hbar/2 pi times kappa, the redshifted acceleration needed to hover at the horizon.
worked_examples.result: kappa = 1/4M and k_B T = hbar kappa/2 pi.

worked_examples.label: Example 28.5
worked_examples.problem: Discuss whether evaporation can run to completion and what spacetime would then look like.
worked_examples.method: Qualitative: note that GR should fail when the hole becomes very small, then provisionally assume it vanishes and present the conformal diagram.
worked_examples.key_insight: The endpoint is beyond classical GR; if the hole disappears, the horizon and singularity are finite in extent and r = 0 becomes an ordinary centre again.
concepts: Penrose diagram of an evaporating black hole
quantum gravity at the end of evaporation

worked_examples.label: Example 28.6
worked_examples.problem: Explain the Unruh effect by transplanting the Hawking pair argument to accelerated observers in flat spacetime.
worked_examples.method: Write the near-horizon metric in Rindler form, identify accelerated world lines with constant x (hyperbolae in X > |T|), treat T = +-X as a horizon, split a pair across T = X, and estimate the temperature by dimensional analysis.
worked_examples.key_insight: Any horizon, even one that exists only because of an observer's acceleration, can split vacuum pairs and produce thermal radiation.
worked_examples.result: k_B T ~ hbar a/c (exact: hbar a/2 pi c).

worked_examples.problem: Margin note 12: which black holes can actually be shrinking today, given that the CMB at 2.73 K heats them?
worked_examples.method: Evaluate the Hawking temperature for one solar mass and solve T(M) = T_CMB for the critical mass.
worked_examples.key_insight: Stellar and supermassive holes are nanokelvin-cold and must keep growing; only holes below roughly 10^-8 solar masses (an asteroid's mass) are hot enough to lose mass now.
worked_examples.result: T(M_sun) ~ 62 nK; M_CMB ~ 2.3 x 10^-8 M_sun ~ 4.5 x 10^22 kg (printed as 10^23 kg).
concepts: black holes in the cosmic microwave background

worked_examples.problem: Identify the entropy of a Schwarzschild hole from its temperature.
worked_examples.method: Treat M as internal energy, differentiate A = 16 pi M^2 to get dM = dA/32 pi M, factor out the Hawking temperature, and compare with dU = T dS (no work).
worked_examples.key_insight: Area is the variable conjugate to temperature, so entropy scales with area, not volume.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A black hole as a thermodynamic black body
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The opening and section 28.2 insist the emission spectrum is exactly that of an ideal thermal radiator, which licenses using Stefan-Boltzmann and thermodynamic laws.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Greybody factors make the spectrum only approximately Planckian far from the hole; heat capacity is negative unlike ordinary bodies.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Overlay a Planck curve at k_B T = hbar/8 pi M with the hole's spectrum as the learner changes M, showing the peak wavelength compared with the horizon size.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Borrowing energy from the vacuum on a short-term loan
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Pair creation is described as borrowing Delta E that must be repaid within a time set by hbar; the horizon lets the loan go unpaid.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Heuristic; in field theory no energy is literally borrowed and the Hawking flux is not a local process at the horizon.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Loan meter: a timer bar for each virtual pair drains; if the partner crosses the horizon before the bar empties, the debt is written off and a photon leaves.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Dictionary between black-hole mechanics and thermodynamics (M as U, kappa as T, A as S, Omega dL and Phi dq as work)
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Four laws are listed in parallel with the ordinary laws and an explicit variable-by-variable table.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: kappa and A correspond to T and S only up to the constant factors hbar/2 pi k_B and k_B/4 hbar; the printed sign of the work terms is inconsistent; the classical area law fails quantum mechanically.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Two-column card flip: tapping a thermodynamic law reveals its black-hole twin with the conversion factors and a physical example.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Hovering near a black hole is like accelerating in empty space
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Near-horizon Schwarzschild is written as Rindler space, so the Hawking argument is rerun across the acceleration horizon.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Unruh radiation is observer-dependent and not a flux reaching inertial detectors; Hawking radiation reaches distant inertial observers. Global structure differs.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Split screen: static observer at height rho above a horizon versus accelerated rocket in flat space with matching acceleration; both thermometers read the same local temperature.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Cooking a steak by accelerating it
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Unruh's quip in margin note 20 conveys that acceleration equals temperature, while the huge acceleration needed shows how tiny the effect is.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Humorous; the printed acceleration has wrong units (should be cm s^-2) and is about an order of magnitude low for 300 C.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Acceleration dial with everyday benchmarks (car, fighter jet, electron in a laser field) and the temperature each would give.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Euclidean near-horizon geometry as a flat plane in polar coordinates with time as the angle
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Exercise 28.4 turns the near-horizon metric into d rho^2 + rho^2 d psi^2 so that the need for a smooth centre forces a period on imaginary time, hence a temperature.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Requires accepting that thermal field theory lives on periodic imaginary time; the Lorentzian meaning of the construction is indirect.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: 3D paper cone: learner chooses the period of psi; unless it is 2 pi the surface shows a cone tip at rho = 0, and the corresponding temperature readout snaps to hbar/8 pi M only when the tip disappears.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Inside the horizon, the time Killing direction behaves like a space direction
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: negative Killing energy inside the horizon
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Since xi is spacelike inside, -p.xi is like a momentum component that can have either sign, so negative values are no more alarming than negative momentum.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only the Killing energy flips sign; locally measured energies remain positive.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Light-cone tilt animation showing xi as an arrow that passes from inside the cone (outside the hole) to outside the cone (inside the hole).

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Black holes can only absorb; nothing ever comes out.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Quantum effects make every black hole radiate thermally, although the radiation is far too weak to observe for astrophysical holes.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Classical GR and popular descriptions define black holes by the fact that light cannot escape.

misconceptions_addressed.correction: All observed particles and antiparticles have positive energy; the negative root of the dispersion relation is reinterpreted as a positive-energy antiparticle with reversed momentum.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Dirac-sea stories and the plus-or-minus square root in E^2 = p^2 + m^2.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Hawking radiation requires particles with negative energy as measured locally.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only the Killing energy -p.xi of the infalling member is negative, which is allowed because xi is spacelike inside the horizon; local observers always measure positive energy.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The hole loses mass, so something with negative energy must fall in, and energy is usually thought of as a single observer-independent number.
concepts: negative Killing energy inside the horizon

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Every black hole in the universe is currently shrinking by Hawking radiation.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Holes colder than the 2.73 K CMB absorb more than they emit; any hole above about 10^-8 solar masses is still growing, even ignoring accretion of gas.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Evaporation is presented for an isolated hole, and the environment is easy to forget.
concepts: black holes in the cosmic microwave background

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A more massive black hole should be hotter, the way more massive main-sequence stars are hotter.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Hawking temperature is inversely proportional to mass; large holes are extraordinarily cold and tiny ones are hot.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Intuition from ordinary lab bodies, which warm up when energy is added, and from the stellar mass-temperature trend; the negative heat capacity of self-gravitating systems is unfamiliar.
concepts: negative heat capacity of black holes

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Shrinking horizon area during evaporation means the second law of thermodynamics is violated.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The area theorem assumes classical matter; the generalized second law counts the radiation's entropy, which at least compensates the loss of horizon entropy.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter first presents dA >= 0 as the second law of black-hole mechanics.

misconceptions_addressed.correction: The book states it has not been measured; for astrophysical holes it is swamped by the CMB and by accretion.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: It is widely discussed as established physics and supported by analogue experiments.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The heuristic estimate hbar/4M is the actual temperature or photon energy.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It sets the scale only; the exact result is k_B T = hbar/8 pi M, smaller by 2 pi, and the spectrum is thermal with mean photon energy of a few k_B T.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The derivation looks clean and produces a definite number.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: An accelerated detector and an inertial one agree on whether particles are present.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In the Unruh effect the accelerated observer sees a thermal bath in the same state that the inertial observer calls empty vacuum; particle number depends on the observer.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In classical physics the presence of a particle is observer-independent.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Surface gravity is the acceleration an astronaut hovering at the horizon would feel.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The locally felt acceleration diverges at the horizon; kappa is that acceleration multiplied by the redshift factor, i.e. the force per unit mass applied from infinity.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The name suggests the Newtonian surface gravity GM/R^2 (which happens to give 1/4M at R = 2M).

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Hawking particles are emitted from the singularity or escape from inside the horizon.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In the heuristic picture the escaping quantum is created outside the horizon; nothing crosses r = 2M outward.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Radiation from a black hole sounds like something leaking out of it.

thought_experiments.name: Plunging interior observer checks an infalling photon
thought_experiments.setup: An observer inside r = 2M moving purely in the r direction (u^t = 0) measures the energy of a radially infalling photon that was half of a vacuum pair.
thought_experiments.lesson: Local positivity only requires p^r < 0, so the photon is unconstrained in p^t and can exist indefinitely, freeing its partner.
concepts: radial plunge with zero Killing energy inside the horizon
thought_experiments.app_idea: Interior Eddington-Finkelstein diagram where the learner aims photons from the plunging observer and sees E_obs colour-coded positive or negative.

thought_experiments.name: Watching one vacuum fluctuation from just above the horizon
thought_experiments.setup: A freely falling frame released from rest at 2M + epsilon watches a photon pair form; the infaller reaches the horizon after about 2(2M epsilon)^{1/2} of proper time while the partner climbs to infinity.
thought_experiments.lesson: Uncertainty sets the local energy, redshift reduces it on the way out, and the height epsilon drops out, leaving hbar/4M.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Slider for epsilon with three linked readouts (fall time, local energy, energy at infinity) showing the last one stays flat.

thought_experiments.name: Merging two black holes
thought_experiments.setup: Two holes collide and form one.
thought_experiments.lesson: Classically, the final horizon area must be at least the sum of the initial areas, limiting how much mass can be radiated.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Merger calculator: choose two masses, see the minimum final mass allowed by area increase and the maximum energy that gravitational waves could carry.

thought_experiments.name: Throwing entropy into a black hole
thought_experiments.setup: Hot matter falls through the horizon so its entropy disappears from view.
thought_experiments.lesson: The hole's mass and area rise, and the generalized second law keeps total entropy from decreasing.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Entropy ledger bar chart: matter entropy, horizon entropy, radiation entropy, and their sum as the learner drops boxes in or lets the hole evaporate.

thought_experiments.name: What happens to information after complete evaporation
thought_experiments.setup: A hole formed from a pure state evaporates entirely, leaving only thermal radiation.
thought_experiments.lesson: Either unitarity fails, or information escapes, or a remnant or final burst stores it; resolving this needs quantum gravity.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Branching storyboard on the evaporating Penrose diagram with the three endings the book lists.

thought_experiments.name: Black hole sitting in the CMB
thought_experiments.setup: A solar-mass hole at 62 nK is bathed in 2.73 K radiation.
thought_experiments.lesson: Net heat flows into the hole, so it grows; only asteroid-mass holes hotter than the CMB can shrink today.
concepts: black holes in the cosmic microwave background
thought_experiments.app_idea: Mass slider with a balance scale of emitted versus absorbed power against a CMB temperature that falls with cosmic time.

thought_experiments.name: Accelerating through empty space
thought_experiments.setup: An observer undergoes constant proper acceleration in the Minkowski vacuum while an inertial observer passes by.
thought_experiments.lesson: Only the accelerated observer, who has a horizon, detects thermal radiation at hbar a/2 pi c k_B.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Rindler wedge animation with a detector click counter that runs only for the accelerated world line.

historical_notes.event: Showed that black holes emit thermal radiation (published 1975).
historical_notes.significance: Turned black holes into thermodynamic objects and opened semiclassical gravity and the information problem.

historical_notes.event: Wrote The Large Scale Structure of Space-Time, recommended by the authors as an advanced, clear and well-illustrated text.
historical_notes.significance: Standard reference for global causal structure and singularity theorems.

historical_notes.event: Placed 25th in a BBC public poll of greatest Britons (the margin note compares Newton, Faraday and Maxwell).
historical_notes.significance: Humorous illustration of his public fame.

historical_notes.event: Held that information falling into an evaporating hole is permanently lost; margin note recalls his mock endorsements for a spoof newspaper.
historical_notes.significance: Records one side of the still-open information debate (Hawking later explored other views, not mentioned).

historical_notes.event: Predicted that accelerated observers see a thermal bath in the vacuum; joked that acceleration could cook a steak.
historical_notes.significance: Showed that thermal effects arise from horizons generally, not only from black holes (the original paper is from 1976, not cited in the book).

applications_and_observations.details: The book notes that no measurement of Hawking radiation exists.

applications_and_observations.topic: Temperature of a solar-mass black hole
applications_and_observations.details: Hawking temperature evaluated for one solar mass is tens of nanokelvin, far below the CMB.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: M_sun = 1.99 x 10^30 kg gives T ~ 62 nK versus T_CMB = 2.73 K.

applications_and_observations.topic: Critical mass for a black hole hotter than the CMB
applications_and_observations.details: Setting T_H = T_CMB defines the mass above which holes cannot currently shrink; gas and dust accretion dominates observed growth anyway.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: M_CMB ~ 2.3 x 10^-8 M_sun; book prints 4.5 x 10^23 kg but 2.3 x 10^-8 M_sun is 4.5 x 10^22 kg (our check).

applications_and_observations.topic: Unruh temperature for a steak-cooking acceleration
applications_and_observations.details: Unruh's joke that a huge acceleration would reach grilling temperatures.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Book: 10^24 cm s^-1 (units should be cm s^-2) for 300 C. Our check with T_U = hbar a/2 pi c k_B: about 1.4 x 10^23 m s^-2 = 1.4 x 10^25 cm s^-2 for 573 K.

applications_and_observations.topic: Evaporation lifetime and primordial black holes (our estimate)
applications_and_observations.details: Not in the book: with photon-only emission, tau = 5120 pi G^2 M^3/(hbar c^4). Useful for tutors to make tau ~ M^3 concrete.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our estimates: tau(M_sun) ~ 2 x 10^67 yr; holes of order 10^11 kg (photons only; about 5 x 10^11 kg with all species) would be finishing evaporation now.

applications_and_observations.topic: Scale of black-hole entropy and surface gravity (our estimate)
applications_and_observations.details: Not in the book: S = k_B A/4 l_P^2 and kappa = c^4/4GM evaluated for one solar mass.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our estimates: S(M_sun) ~ 10^77 k_B; kappa(M_sun) ~ 1.5 x 10^13 m s^-2; Unruh temperature at a = g ~ 4 x 10^-20 K.

applications_and_observations.details: The second law of black-hole mechanics requires a merged hole to have at least the combined horizon area of its progenitors.

notation_and_conventions.convention: G = c = 1, with hbar and k_B written explicitly (e.g. k_B T = hbar/8 pi M, S = A k_B/4 hbar); c is restored in the Unruh temperature hbar a/(2 pi c k_B).
notation_and_conventions.notes: Mixed practice; learners should restore constants when quoting numbers.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Tilde marks conserved energy and angular momentum per unit rest mass; E without tilde is total energy -xi.p.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Margin note 6 spells out the distinction.

notation_and_conventions.convention: E_obs = -p.u is energy measured by a local observer; superscript infinity denotes energy measured by the static observer at infinity, -p.xi.
Bold xi = e_t with components (1,0,0,0) in Schwarzschild coordinates and also (1,0,0,0) as partial_V in ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates (V, r, theta, phi).
Semicolon for covariant derivative, comma for partial; X_{alpha;mu} = X_{alpha,mu} - Gamma^sigma_{alpha mu} X_sigma.
M mass, L angular momentum (not J), q charge, A horizon area, kappa surface gravity, Omega horizon angular velocity, Phi horizon electric potential.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Many references use J and Q.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Lower-case (t, x) are Rindler coordinates with ds^2 = -x^2 dt^2 + dx^2; upper-case (T, X) are Minkowski with ds^2 = -dT^2 + dX^2.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Acceleration parameter set to 1 in the Rindler form.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Margin note 17 states dW = -p dV and maps Omega dL and Phi dq to -dW.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Internally inconsistent with dU = T dS - p dV; the work terms should correspond to +dW (work done on the hole).

notation_and_conventions.convention: t = -i t_E, with t_E = 4M psi in Exercise 28.4.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The italic text writes i t_E = hbar/k_B T; what is meant is that the period of t_E equals hbar/k_B T.

margin_notes.summary: Chapter epigraph: a short line from the novelist Henry Fielding about nature sharing a single grin, a playful nod to the universality (thermal, horizon-independent) of the results to come.
Recommends Hawking and Ellis's advanced book for clarity and diagrams, and jokes about Hawking's 25th place in a BBC poll of great Britons compared with Newton, Faraday, Maxwell and an actor.
Corrects the idea that antiparticles have negative energy by reinterpreting the negative-energy root as a positive-energy antiparticle with reversed three-momentum.
Uses the wavefunction phase exp(-iEt/hbar) to show that positive energy forward in time is equivalent to negative energy backward in time, linking energy sign to causality.
Explains that the u^t = 0 interior path is timelike because r is the time direction inside the horizon.
Recalls the photon effective energy equation and that for zero angular momentum E-tilde equals plus or minus p^r.
Identifies the static observer at infinity with the Killing vector and distinguishes E-tilde (per unit mass) from E = -xi.p.
Shows xi.xi = g_tt changes sign at r = 2M.
Stresses that the observer at infinity measures locally and never measures the negative Killing energy of the infalling particle.
Recalls the radial energy equation with effective potential and derives eqn 28.3 for zero angular momentum, giving E-tilde for a frame at rest at 2M + epsilon.
Recalls E-tilde = -xi.u = -u_t.
CMB feeding: holes colder than 2.73 K must grow; solar-mass hole is at 62 nK; only holes lighter than about 2.3 x 10^-8 solar masses can shrink today (kg value misprinted by a factor of ten).

Defines a Killing horizon as a null hypersurface where a Killing field has zero norm and interprets surface gravity as the force per unit mass applied at infinity to hold an object at the horizon; points to Poisson for proofs.
Gives the lowered Killing components in ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates, noting the field is null on the horizon.
Points to Chapter 39 for more on thermodynamics.
Lists the four ordinary laws of thermodynamics for comparison with the black-hole laws.
Tabulates the correspondence M-U, kappa-T, A-S and rotational and electric terms with work.
Recommends review articles on black-hole thermodynamics by Page (2005) and Carlip (2014).
Anecdote about Hawking's mock quotes for a spoof newspaper.
Unruh's quip about cooking a steak by acceleration and the enormous acceleration required.
Reminds the reader that Minkowski coordinates are (T, X) with ds^2 = -dT^2 + dX^2 in the Rindler discussion.
Exercise 28.4 includes an italic aside on Wick rotation to periodic imaginary time as the route to temperature in field theory, citing Zee.

difficulty.notes: Algebra in Examples 28.1-28.4 is short, but the conceptual content (virtual particles, Killing energy sign flips, horizon thermodynamics, information loss, observer-dependent particles) is subtle and presented heuristically with the rigorous calculation only quoted. Surface gravity and Exercise 28.4 need comfort with covariant derivatives, Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates and Wick rotation. Several printed slips (lifetime formula, eqn 28.12 reference, M_CMB power of ten, eqn 28.23, work-term signs, Unruh units, d theta squared) can confuse careful readers.
