teaching_gems.gem: Estimate the Hawking energy by combining the uncertainty-limited energy of a pair near 2M + epsilon with the redshift to infinity, and watch epsilon cancel.
teaching_gems.why_effective: One quantum ingredient plus familiar GR tools yields hbar/M scaling with no free parameter, making a deep result feel inevitable.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Epsilon slider with three coupled bars (fall time, local energy, energy at infinity); the last bar stays fixed and shows hbar/4M next to the exact hbar/8 pi M.

teaching_gems.gem: Separate the locally measured energy -p.u (always positive) from the Killing energy -p.xi (sign-indefinite once xi is spacelike).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Resolves the negative-energy puzzle geometrically and reinforces what conserved quantities do and do not mean.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Plot g_tt(r) crossing zero at 2M with light cones overlaid; drag a momentum vector and see -p.u and -p.xi update with signs.

teaching_gems.gem: Derive entropy by writing dM in terms of dA and pulling out the Hawking temperature, so area is read off as entropy.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A two-line calculation turns an analogy into a formula and makes 'entropy proportional to area' concrete.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Step-through derivation card where learner fills the missing factor at each line with instant feedback.

teaching_gems.gem: Scale argument: T proportional to 1/M and A proportional to M^2 give L proportional to M^-2 and lifetime proportional to M^3.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Pure proportional reasoning from a black-body law gives evaporation dynamics and highlights negative heat capacity.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Evaporation simulator plotting M(t) and T(t) with log axes, an optional CMB bath whose temperature falls with cosmic time, and markers for primordial-mass holes.

teaching_gems.gem: Compare the Hawking temperature of real black holes with the CMB to show that astrophysical holes grow.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Grounds an abstract formula in numbers and corrects a popular misconception.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Mass slider spanning asteroid to supermassive with a temperature needle against a 2.73 K line.

teaching_gems.gem: Line up the laws of black-hole mechanics with the laws of thermodynamics in parallel columns plus a dictionary.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Structural parallel is memorable and lets learners predict each law from its thermodynamic twin.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Matching game pairing laws and variables, then revealing conversion factors hbar/2 pi and k_B/4 hbar.

teaching_gems.gem: Near the horizon Schwarzschild looks like Rindler space, so Hawking radiation is the black-hole version of the Unruh effect.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Unifies two effects under one idea (horizons are hot) and reuses familiar flat-spacetime diagrams.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Zoom animation from a Kruskal diagram into the neighbourhood of the bifurcation point until it becomes the Rindler wedge of Fig. 28.3.

teaching_gems.gem: Euclidean trick: after Wick rotation the near-horizon plane is flat polar space, and demanding no cone tip gives the exact temperature.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A purely geometric smoothness requirement produces the 8 pi that heuristic arguments miss.
teaching_gems.app_idea: 3D cone that flattens into a smooth disc only when the imaginary-time period equals 8 pi M; the temperature readout updates with the chosen period.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The opening paragraph writes the pair lifetime as Delta t ~ Delta E/hbar, which is dimensionally wrong; the correct hbar/Delta E appears later.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confusion about whether larger borrowed energy means longer or shorter lifetimes.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State Delta t ~ hbar/Delta E and emphasize that energetic fluctuations are briefer.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The pair-splitting argument (Examples 28.1-28.2) is heuristic: it treats a single virtual photon classically, claims p^t is unconstrained, calls p^t a flat-spacetime component, and does not explain the thermal spectrum. The real derivation uses mode mixing between past and future vacua.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think Hawking radiation is derived here or that emission is localized at the horizon.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Label the argument as a plausibility estimate, show that its output is the redshift factor at work, and give a qualitative account of the Bogoliubov picture for advanced learners.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eqn 28.11 is written with an approximately-equal sign and the text equates the typical photon energy with k_B T; the relation is exact and the mean photon energy is about 2.7 k_B T.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Uncertainty about what is exact and misreading of the spectrum.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Write k_B T = hbar c^3/8 pi G M exactly and show a Planck curve.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Margin note 12 cites eqn 28.12 for the Hawking temperature (it should be 28.11) and gives M_CMB = 4.5 x 10^23 kg, which is ten times the value corresponding to 2.3 x 10^-8 solar masses.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners reproducing the numbers get mismatched answers.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use M_CMB ~ 4.5 x 10^22 kg and reference eqn 28.11.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed eqn 28.23 for the heat capacity, -hbar^2/(16 pi k_B T^2), does not follow from S = k_B A/4 hbar and k_B T = hbar/8 pi M, which give C = -hbar/(8 pi k_B T^2) = -2S.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Students cannot reach the stated answer and may doubt a correct calculation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Provide the corrected result, and discuss the sign physically.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Margin note 17 claims dW = -p dV yet maps Omega dL and Phi dq to -dW, which conflicts with dU = T dS - p dV; also kappa and A correspond to T and S only up to constants.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Sign confusion when extending the first law to rotating and charged holes.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Write dM = T dS + Omega dJ + Phi dQ with T = hbar kappa/2 pi k_B and S = k_B A/4 hbar, and treat the last two terms as work done on the hole.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The area theorem is stated without its energy-condition hypothesis ('as a function of cosmic time' is vague), so its violation by evaporation looks arbitrary.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think the area law is broken by fiat.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Explain that Hawking radiation's negative energy flux into the hole violates the null energy condition the theorem assumes, which is why the generalized second law is needed.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Surface gravity's normalization dependence and its meaning as a redshifted acceleration are left to a margin note; the phrase 'suitably chosen linear combination of Killing vectors' is only relevant for rotating holes.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may equate kappa with the local acceleration at the horizon, which is infinite.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show that local proper acceleration times the redshift factor tends to 1/4M as r approaches 2M.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Unruh margin note gives acceleration in cm s^-1 (should be cm s^-2) and the number is roughly an order of magnitude below what T_U = hbar a/2 pi c k_B gives for 300 C.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Quote a ~ 10^23 m s^-2 for a few hundred kelvin and compare with a = g giving 4 x 10^-20 K.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise 28.4 has a missing square in d Omega^2 and writes i t_E = hbar/k_B T instead of stating that the period of t_E equals hbar/k_B T; the no-conical-singularity reasoning is left implicit.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers without QFT background do not know why psi must have period 2 pi.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show a cone versus a flat disc and state the smoothness condition explicitly.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Bekenstein (area-entropy, 1973) and Bardeen, Carter and Hawking (four laws, 1973) are not credited, and there is no mention of greybody factors, particle species, or the statistical origin of entropy.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a short timeline and a note that entropy counting is a test for quantum gravity candidates.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Information-loss discussion is dated: no mention of complementarity, firewalls, the Page curve or recent island calculations, and Hawking's later views are not noted.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think the debate stalled with remnants and explosions.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a brief modern update framed as ongoing research, clearly marked beyond the book.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Fig. 28.1 draws horizons as vertical timelike lines with a timelike singularity between them, unlike the causal structure of Schwarzschild.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: May reinforce a picture in which one could hover inside the horizon or the singularity is a place in space.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Redraw on Eddington-Finkelstein or Penrose diagrams with light cones.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The chapter summary says the pair is created 'at' the event horizon, while section 28.1 and Example 28.2 place it just outside (at 2M + epsilon); the Unruh example likewise creates it on T = X.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may picture particles materializing on the horizon itself, where no static observer exists, and lose the role of the small but finite epsilon in the estimate.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say 'straddling' or 'just outside' the horizon and point out that the final answer is independent of how close.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'If nothing escapes a black hole, how could it possibly shine?' Let the learner propose that something happens just outside, then introduce vacuum pairs.

Before Example 28.1 check that the learner can distinguish -p.u (what a local observer measures) from -p.xi (a conserved number that only equals measured energy for a static observer far away). This distinction unlocks the whole section.

Recommended order: vacuum pairs, horizon splitting picture, local positivity, sign of xi.xi across r = 2M, epsilon estimate, exact temperature, evaporation scaling, CMB comparison, surface gravity, entropy, laws, generalized second law, information, Unruh.
When doing Example 28.2 ask the learner to predict how the answer depends on epsilon before computing; then point out that the product -g^{tt} E-tilde is just the familiar redshift factor.
Always restore units when giving numbers: T = 6 x 10^-8 K (M_sun/M), and warn that the chapter's heuristic gives a value 2 pi too large.
Check understanding with a sign question: if you add mass to a black hole, does it get hotter or colder? Follow up with why this makes evaporation a runaway (negative heat capacity).
Use the CMB margin note to dismantle 'black holes are evaporating now'; ask the learner to find the mass at which T_H equals 2.73 K.

For surface gravity, first give the physical meaning (force per unit mass applied from far away to hold a mass at the horizon), then the Killing definition, then the Eddington-Finkelstein computation, and only for advanced learners walk through Exercise 28.3.
Correct the printed slips proactively when a learner works from the book: lifetime hbar/Delta E, M_CMB ~ 4.5 x 10^22 kg, C = -hbar/(8 pi k_B T^2), d theta^2, Unruh acceleration units.

Common learner question: 'Does the infalling particle really have negative energy?' Answer: locally no; only its Killing energy is negative, which is permitted because inside the horizon that quantity behaves like a momentum component.

Common learner question: 'Would I see Hawking radiation if I hovered near the horizon?' Link to the Unruh effect: a hovering observer is accelerating and sees a hot local bath whose temperature, redshifted to infinity, gives the Hawking temperature.
Common learner question: 'Where does the information go?' Present the three options the book lists, say it is unresolved, and flag modern work as beyond the text.
For learners with QFT background, Exercise 28.4 is the most rewarding route to the exact 8 pi; for others, show the cone-versus-disc picture without the Wick rotation algebra.
